Because of this they grew resentful and went astray. Some of them were converted later by Abibos, bishop of Nekresi, and some of them have remained in paganism to this day.
Then Saint Nino set out to go to Ran, to convert Peroz. When she came near Kukheti, to the village of Bodi, she stayed there for some days.
And a multitude of people came to her from Kakheti. They questioned her and confessed her teaching.
Then she fell ill there. When Rev, the king's son, and his wife Salome, who lived at Ujarma, learned of it, they came to Nino and told the king and queen.
The king and queen sent Bishop John to bring Saint Nino back, but Saint Nino would not agree.
Then the king himself went, with a multitude of people. And a multitude of powerful people gathered around her.
For all the people looked on Nino's face as on the face of a heavenly angel. They tore pieces from the hem of her garment,
took them and kissed them in faith. And all the noblewomen sitting around her pleaded with her urgently,
with tears flowing from their eyes because they were being parted from their teacher, who had laboured for them, and the skilled healer of the sick.
And Salome of Ujarma and Perozhavri of Sivnia spoke to her, and with them the eristavis
and the princes asked her: "Where, or from what place, did you come to this land to be our saviour? Or where were you brought up, lady? Tell us your story.
Why do you speak of captivity, blessed deliverer of captives? For we have learned this from you: that there were prophets before the Son of God,
and after him the twelve apostles and the other seventy. And to us God sent no one except you. So how can you say, 'I am a captive,' or a stranger?"
Then Saint Nino began to speak and said: "Daughters of the faith, my dear noble ladies,
I see that all of you, like those first women, are founded on faith in Christ, and you wish to know the ways of me, a poor handmaid.
Now I will tell you, for my soul has now come up to my throat, and I am falling asleep forever with the sleep of my mother.
So take writing materials and write down my poor and lowly life, so that your children too may know of your faith, of how you took me in, and of the miracles of God that you have seen."
Then Salome of Ujarma and Perozhavri of Sivnia quickly took writing materials. Saint Nino began to speak, and they wrote it down.
And she told them the whole life of that holy and blessed woman, which we have written above.
And she commended the priest Jacob to the king, so that he would become bishop after John.
Then Bishop John celebrated the liturgy and gave Saint Nino communion of the body and blood of Christ.
And she commended her soul to the King of heaven in the fourteenth year after she came to Kartli,
in the 338th year after the Ascension of Christ, and the 5838th year from the beginning of the world.
Then both of these cities, Mtskheta and Ujarma, and all of Kartli were shaken by the death of Nino.
They went there and buried her victory-clad body in that very place, in Kukheti, in the village of Bodbe (Bodi). She herself had asked the king to be buried there, by the providence of God.
The saint did this out of humility, because that place was held in no regard.
The king and all the nobles were grieved that she was buried there, but they buried her there to fulfil her command and her testament.
When the God-enlightened King Mirian had accomplished all this, he established all Kartli and Hereti in the faith of the Holy Trinity,
the God who is one in essence and without beginning, the Creator of all. And they were established in the perfect faith.
At that time Mirian's son, named Bakar, was a hostage with the emperor Constantine. King Constantine sent him back with great gifts and wrote as follows:
"I, Constantine, king and autocrat, a new servant of the King of heaven, once taken captive by the devil and afterwards redeemed by the Creator,
have written to you, the God-enlightened believing King Mirian, newly planted in the faith as I am. Peace and joy be with you!
Since you have come to know the Trinity, one in essence, God without beginning, Creator of all, I no longer need a hostage from you.
It is enough for us to have as mediator between us Christ, the Son of God, born before the ages, who became man for our salvation, and his precious Cross,
which has been given to us as a guide, to those who trust in him with their heart. Through the mediation of God the Creator, let us remain in brotherly love.
I have given your son back to you: see him and rejoice. May the angel of peace sent from God be with you always.
May God the Creator drive the deceiving devil out of your borders."
Bakar, the son of King Mirian, came to Mtskheta together with King Constantine's envoy.
King Mirian and Queen Nana were filled with joy and gave thanks to God, the giver of perfect gifts.
Then King Mirian finished building the episcopal church and celebrated its consecration with great glory.

In the twenty-fifth year after King Mirian's conversion, his son Rev died. Rev was the son-in-law of Tiridates (Trdat), king of the Armenians, and the kingship had been given to him during his lifetime.
They buried him in the tomb that Rev himself had built. In that same year King Mirian fell ill, and he died of this illness.
He called his son Bakar and his wife Nana, and said to Nana: "Behold, I am going back to where I came from. I give thanks to the most merciful God,
Creator of heaven and earth, who rescued me, a captive of the devil, from the mouth of hell, and made me worthy to be with him at his right hand.
You, Nana, if you are granted more time to live after my life ends, divide our royal treasury in two and take half to the tomb of Nino,
our enlightener, because times change, so that that place may never be shaken. For it is a seat of kings, yet it is poor."
Likewise he charged the bishops to magnify the glory of that place, "for it is worthy of honour." And to his son he said:
"My child, my darkness has been changed into light and my death into life. I have given you the crown of my kingship.
May God, the Creator of heaven and earth, establish you in the perfect faith.
Exert yourself in all the commandments of the Son of God, and stand firm in them completely. For the name of Christ, count death as life, for by it one gains imperishable
life. And wherever you find those idols, the passions of fire [?], burn them with fire, and make those who trusted in them drink the ashes.
And command this to your sons as well, for I know that they [the idols] will come to an end even among the Caucasians.
But you, follow this with your heart, and entrust yourself to the Son of God, who was born before the ages, became man, and suffered for our salvation.
And by carrying the precious Cross before you, defeat your enemies, as it is accustomed to do for those who trust in him with their heart.
And honour that living Pillar raised up by God, and let your hope be wholly in it, and let your departure be into eternal sleep in the faith of the Trinity."
And he had the cross of Saint Nino brought, which he had possessed from the beginning, and he hung the royal crown on that cross.
And he had his son Bakar brought, and traced the sign of the cross on his head; and he took the crown from the cross and set it on his son's head.
And King Mirian died and was buried in the upper church, by the middle pillar on the south side, on its northern side.
And within that pillar is a portion of the Pillar raised up by God.
And in the second year Queen Nana died and was buried at that same pillar, on the west side, where King Mirian had been buried.
The twenty-fifth king, Bakar, son of Mirian, a Khosroid. And his son Bakar sat as king, and he was a believer like his father.
And he converted most of the Caucasians whom his father had not been able to convert. And enmity arose between him and the Armenians.
For the Armenians wanted the kingship of Kartli for Bakar's nephew, the son of Rev, the daughter's son of Trdat, king of the Armenians.
But this Bakar negotiated with the king of the Persians, his father's brother's son, submitted to him, and exchanged land with his sister's son Peroz,
who held Ran as far as Bardav, given to him by Mirian; and in its place he gave him the lands from Samshvilde onward as far as
the head of the Abotsi. Only then were Peroz and his people baptized. And they gathered forces from the Khosroids and fought the Armenians in Javakheti: they defeated and routed the Armenians.
Then King Bakar, through the mediation of the king of the Greeks and the king of the Persians, had a written deed drawn up by his nephews and their mother Salome, as follows:
"As long as there is a descendant of Bakar who is able to hold the kingship, the kingship shall be his, and the descendants of Rev shall never seek the kingship."
Only then did he bring his nephews and give them Kukheti, and he installed them in Rustavi as eristavis.
This Bakar spent all the days of his life in great faith, and he increased the number of priests and deacons throughout Kartli and Ran to serve the churches.
He built the church of Tsilkani. He died and was buried beside his brother.
The twenty-sixth king, Mirdat, son of Bakar, a Khosroid. And his son Mirdat sat as king, and he reigned in great faith.
And he built a church in the fortress of Tukharisi, because there was no church in the gorge of Klarjeti, and there he appointed priests as teachers for the Klarjians.
And he added to the adornment and building of the churches of Erusheti and Tsunda.
Then, during the reign of this Mirdat, the Georgians began to take pieces from the Life-giving Pillar and make them into crosses,
for great miracles and healings took place wherever there was a piece of the Life-giving Pillar.
King Mirdat did not prevent them from taking pieces, because the true bishop Jacob had also judged it fitting, and he said:
"It has been granted by the Lord, and it is fitting to make that God-raised pillar into the form of a cross."
And pieces of the Life-giving Pillar spread to every place in Kartli.
Then this King Mirdat made a cross of moderate size from that same pillar, and around what remained of the Life-giving Pillar he built a casing of stone and mortar,
and he raised the masonry as high as the original pillar; and on top of that pillar he set up the cross, the life-giving wood.
And he spent all the days of his life without disturbance, in great faith.
In his time Bishop Jacob died, and Job the Armenian, deacon of Catholicos Nerses, took the see. And King Mirdat died.
The twenty-seventh king, Varaz-Bakar, son of Mirdat. A Khosroid; and his son Varaz-Bakar took the throne as king.
He took two wives: one was the daughter of Trdat, son of Rev, grandson of Mirian; the other was the granddaughter of Peroz, grandchild of Mirian's daughter.

He was childless, for he had no son or offspring, and he kept praying to God with fasting and fervent supplication that he might be found worthy to be given a son, which he was in fact found worthy to receive.
For at one time, as he was coming from the provinces to his royal seat, Mtskheta, he stopped for the evening on the bank of the great river called the Mtkvari (Kura).
And when he had finished the evening prayer so that he could go to sleep (for he never ate or slept without prayer),
During this prayer a shining angel of light appeared to him, and the king was afraid at the sight of him. But the angel said to him:
"Do not be afraid, O king, for your supplications have been heard before God. A son will be given to you who will be great and perfect before God and men, and he will turn many peoples to God."
When the king woke up, he glorified God with a joyful spirit.
After a short time the king's wife conceived and bore him a son, and the king, together with his whole kingdom, held a great celebration
at the time of his birth. They baptized him in the name of the Holy Trinity and gave him the name Murvanos.
So this saint was born through the announcement of an angel, like Samuel and Jeremiah. And he was made holy from the womb, like the great Forerunner.
When he was given over to be taught, in a short time he learned all of Scripture, and
he would read it with understanding and study it day and night, for he was alert and sharp of mind, and the grace of God was upon him.
In the time of Theodosius the Younger, emperor of the Greeks, hostility arose between the Greeks and the Persians;

and Emperor Theodosius, fearing that the Georgians might join the Persians and the Greeks be defeated, therefore asked the king of the Georgians for friendship, and for greater security he also asked for hostages.
And so that the Georgians would not be separated from the Greeks, the king of the Georgians granted every request of the emperor of the Greeks,
And he sent his son Murvanos, who was fourteen years old, as a hostage to the city of Constantinople, together with other royal children, with great honor and glory.
And when they arrived and King Theodosius learned of it, he brought him up to the royal palace with much [?].
And as soon as they saw him, King Theodosius and his wife Eudocia, together with their whole court, greeted him with longing, love and kisses, as though he were a son given to them by God.
When the boy Murvanos saw that the king, the queen and the whole palace lived in great devotion to God, with fasting, prayer
and almsgiving to the poor, he made his own spiritual struggle all the greater: much fasting, boundless vigils, unceasing prayer, almsgiving to the poor, gentleness,
love, kindness and patience. He came to delight in all the fruits of the Spirit, which are the holy virtues, according to the word of the holy apostle.
But more and above all else, he gained purity of soul and body, like the great Joseph.
In a short time he learned the Greek language and all church and philosophical learning.
Likewise, when he went to Jerusalem, he came to the Lord's tomb. There he was tonsured as a monk, and they gave him the name Peter.
He learned the Syriac language and Syriac learning, so that everyone marveled at the prudence and sharpness of his mind.
Every day he divided the allowance he received from the palace among the poor. Under his royal clothes he wore rough, coarse haircloth.
He would fast for two days at a time, three days at a time, and even a whole week at a time.
For he was a great saint before God, and through a vision and command of Christ he became bishop of Maiuma,
for no one was able to praise him except Gregory the Dialogist, patriarch of Rome, who wrote his praise in his book.
Through an angel's announcement, a son was granted to this man, and they named him Murvanos.
Like the Forerunner, this Murvanos was a great saint from the womb, and he learned all of the divine Scripture.
And he grew in stature and in grace before God.
When he was twelve years old, Theodosius, king of the Greeks, became somewhat afraid that the Georgians might join the Persians, and he asked Varaz-Bakar for Murvanos as a hostage.
He took him to Constantinople and raised him in great luxury, like his own son.
But Murvanos did not care at all about the glory of this world. Instead he gave himself even more to prayer and fasting, and lived in purity.
Next to his skin he wore haircloth made of goat hair, and with it he punished his body.
He quickly learned the Greek and Syriac languages and the whole of philosophy, so that everyone marveled.
God gave him gifts of healing the sick, and these are written down in his full Life.
On the night of Epiphany he was standing [?], and he told his servant to bring oil to light the lamp.
But the servant treated Murvanos with contempt and scolded him: "You are a king's son, yet you have no desire for royal things, and you live like a monk, going hungry from Sunday to Sunday":
But Murvanos lit water in a lamp, without oil, and prayed in this way: for seven nights the lamp burned on that water.
And the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him and promised to be with him always. He performed many miracles by means of that lamp, by anointing the sick.
Now there was a certain eunuch of the king. These two agreed together to leave.
King Theodosius learned of it and set guards over them. But with the Lord guiding them, they got through the night and left.
For a pillar of light went before them, as it had for the Israelites, and they heard a voice from the pillar: "Whoever follows me shall not walk in darkness."
They found a ship and travelled for some days. But in a certain city someone seized them, and they were put in prison.
But that night there was an earthquake, thunderbolts and much lightning. A certain man stood over the ruler of the city and spoke to him terrifyingly:
"Release the servants of God. If you do not, this city will be destroyed." Terrified, he released them. After this they came to Jerusalem.
A certain king named Pinianus, who had come from the Roman dominions, was there with his wife. They had left behind the vanity of the world and were living there.
For they had become monastics and had built two monasteries, one for each of them to live in.
These two took them in. After this they went to the Tomb of the Lord, and there they were tonsured as monks.
They named Murvanos Peter and named the eunuch John. Their struggles and labours are beyond telling. They built monasteries and a hostel for strangers.
After this the devil tempted Peter. He reproached him for leaving his ancestral kingdom and for not living well as a monk. But Peter rebuked him and drove him away.
After this Christ appeared to him again and showed him a church in the heavens, with [?] men singing who were beautiful to look at.
And he promised him eternal glory. Then the Patriarch Anastasius forced him to be ordained a priest.
Afterwards he went out into the deserts and built monasteries there as well. While he was staying on the bank of the Jordan, he healed a raging madman.
He travelled through all the deserts of Egypt and of Scetis and performed many miracles.
He returned again to his own monastery and hostel. During a famine, his prayer filled all the containers: the flour bin, the pea bin, the oil jar and the wine jar.
At that time the bishop of Maiuma died. The men of that city gathered and asked for Peter the Iberian.
But he would not accept it in obedience to the patriarch. Instead, he wanted to throw himself down from a height and in that way escape to other places. But
Christ appeared again with a multitude of angels, and at the word of the Lord he accepted the office of bishop.
Many times a voice from above was heard in that city, saying to Peter the Iberian: [?]
He brought rain in times of drought and gave children to the childless. He healed the sick, made barren land fruitful and gave fishermen success.
God also gave him the grace of prophecy and of vision by the Holy Spirit.
For when the souls of Father Isaiah and of Father Zeno of Scetis left their bodies, he saw them rising up to heaven.
After this he learned of his departure from the body, and he told everyone.
And a certain brother, Athanasius, saw a vision concerning Peter: the saints were entreating God,
"Command that Peter the Georgian be brought to us, for he has greatly mortified his flesh."
And after ten days He commanded his coming; after this, for ten days he prayed in his cell.
And on the tenth day he came out and offered the holy sacrifice, and he partook of the holy mysteries, and he gave communion to the others as well, and blessed them and gave them peace.
He went into his cell, lay down and fell asleep in death, on the second of the month of December.
And certain holy men saw his holy soul being led into the multitude of the saints, with hymns and glorification,
whom the priest-martyr Peter of Alexandria led at their head. And many sick people who touched his holy body were healed, as is written in his Life.
Great praise of this blessed man was written by Gregory the Dialogist, the holy patriarch of Rome, in his book. But let us return to our former account.
And Rev's granddaughter bore two sons, whose names were Mirdat and Trdat; Peroz's granddaughter bore one, whose name was Pharasmanes.
This King Varaz-Bakur was a faithless man and a hater of the faith, but he did not dare to make his hatred of the faith known before the people,
for Kartli had been converted, and the nobles and all the people of Kartli were steadfast in great faith. And
for fear of them Varaz-Bakur could not openly abandon the faith. He built no church anywhere, nor did he add anything to those already built, and in everything he behaved lawlessly.
At this the king of the Persians sent an eristavi with a great army against the Armenians and the Georgians to impose tribute.
Then the Armenians sent an envoy to Varaz-Bakur and told him that they should unite and obtain forces from the Greeks,
and open the gates of the Caucasus, and bring out the Ossetians and the Lezgians, and resist the Persians.
And his own nobles also urged him to resist the Persians. He listened neither to the Armenians nor to his own nobles,
for he was faint-hearted [?] and fearful. He withdrew into the valley of Kakheti, built a fortress at Khidari, and strengthened the fortified towns, and he commanded everyone to hide the crosses.
And the Persians came first to Armenia and laid Armenia waste, and they entered Kartli, and the Persian eristavi built a fortress at the gates of Tbilisi, as a fortress for Mtskheta.
Then Varaz-Bakur sent word to him in submission and asked for peace. But the Persian eristavi said to him:
"First give me Ran and Movakan, for they belong to the borders of Persia, and they belong to those who are fully sons of the Persian kings and sit on the thrones of their fathers;
and Kartli is enough for you, who are born of a slave-woman. Keep Kartli, then, and pay tribute to the Khosroid kings."
Then Varaz-Bakur could give no answer for great fear; he gave up Ran and Movakan and agreed to a fixed tribute. And the Persian eristavi handed over the fortress of Tbilisi and departed.
And from then on the Armenians and the Georgians became tributaries of the Persians. And after this the Klarjians broke away from Varaz-Bakur and joined the Greeks.
And the Greeks seized Tukharisi and all of Klarjeti from the sea to Arsiani. And Kartli, without Klarjeti, remained to Varaz-Bakur, together with Hereti and Egrisi.

That same Persian eristavi (governor) led away into captivity the children of Peroz, the daughter's sons of Mirian, the believing king, and he gave their land, the borderland of Kartli, to Varaz-Bakar himself.
And Varaz-Bakar died, and his three young sons were left, who were not able to hold the kingship.
The twenty-eighth king: Trdat, father-in-law of Varaz-Bakar, a Khosroid. Then the nobles of Kartli took counsel and set up as king the father-in-law of Varaz-Bakar,
the son of Rev and grandson of Mirian, an old man named Trdat. They gave him the children of Varaz-Bakar, his daughter's sons, to bring up.
But the third son, the son of the second wife, was brought up by the eristavi of Samshvilde. His name was Pharsman.
This aged Trdat reigned well. He was a believing man, wise and prudent. By his wisdom he pacified the Persians, set up crosses, and furnished the churches.
During his reign Bishop Jacob died, and he appointed Elijah in his place. And he paid tribute to the king of the Persians.
He founded Rustavi and built a church there, and he also built the church of Nekresi. He reigned without disturbance and died in great faith.
The twenty-ninth king: Pharsman, son of Varaz-Bakar, a Khosroid. The son of Varaz-Bakar, great-grandson of Peroz, named Pharsman, took the throne as king,
for he was the eldest of his brothers. Bishop Elijah died, and they appointed Simon. This Pharsman was a believing man and a bold warrior. He entered into negotiations
with the king of the Greeks and asked him for help, and the emperor granted his request. Then he rebelled and no longer paid tribute to the Persians.
He set up many crosses, restored the churches throughout Kartli, and built the church of Bolnisi. He reigned for a short time and died.
The thirtieth king: Mirdat, brother of King Pharsman, a Khosroid. His brother Mirdat took the throne as king. He was the daughter's son of Trdat
and the son of Varaz-Bakar, a Bakarid on his father's side and a Revid on his mother's side, so descended from both sons of Mirian. This Mirdat was a wicked man,
a bold warrior, unbelieving and without fear of God, insolent and arrogant, and he trusted in his own military strength.
He did not serve God. He built no church and added nothing to the churches already built.
In his insolence he made himself an enemy of both the Greeks and the Persians. He demanded Klarjeti, the borderland of Kartli, from the Greeks, and he would not pay tribute to the Persians.
Then the king of the Persians sent an eristavi named Uprob with a strong army against Mirdat.
Then Mirdat, in his insolence, did not shrink from the great number of the Persians. With a small army he went out to meet them at Gardabani and joined battle.
The Persians routed him and took him captive. They came into Kartli, seized Kartli, and ravaged the churches.
But the members of the royal family remained in the gorge of Kakheti, and Bishop Simon was with them. They took Mirdat away to Baghdad, and he died there.
